rationale: B wins because it keeps the good press shapes and throws the hand grenades back over the fence instead of carrying them into the pitch. A keeps an invented contrarian line — "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" — which is exactly the sort of clever-sounding overreach that gets murdered in a reporter's inbox. B's strongest sentence is its discipline: "Without a bank willing to be identified, this becomes a claim the reporter cannot check and the angle should be shelved." That is useful PR judgment, not decoration.
gaps_in_A: "Notion against Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace" imports a competitive fight the update did not supply. It may be true in the world, but it is not grounded in this brief.

"The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" invents a cleaner before/after than the facts support. The update says regulated buyers previously could not adopt and four top banks run pilots; it does not prove the same bank banned use and then reversed course.

"A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" is the big sin: a neat contrarian headline built on an unsupplied claim about Notion's history and SaaS ideology.

"compliance features are usually a paid tier" and "arrive inside the existing Enterprise plan" overstate the pricing fact. The brief only says no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans, not that every new control is bundled for all buyers.
gaps_in_B: "Notion's 100 million users could not get it past bank and hospital compliance" is too broad. The bank proof is supplied; the hospital proof is not.
"It just shipped the checklist" makes the controls sound complete before the proof is in. Residency, processing, backups, telemetry, local offline cache, and key custody still need hard answers.
"Story type: exec-spotlight" is the wrong label for the offline angle. The facts support an engineering deep dive, not an executive profile.

B leaves the pricing fact underused. It rightly refuses "security tax," but a narrower angle around "no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans" could survive with competitor pricing proof and careful caveats.
